claims.text: Above 900 K, thermally activated lattice disordering causes the friction-coefficient spike and loss of wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu/Cu.
The high-temperature deformation mode transitions from dislocation-mediated plasticity to amorphous shear banding rather than merely softening existing dislocations.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating initially has a stable FCC lattice at 300 K.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating has a low dislocation density.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibits short-range order at 300 K.
Oxidation resistance is a known limitation in similar high-entropy alloys above 600 °C.
Rapid lattice disorder occurs in the FeNiCrCoCu/Cu system between 900 K and 1200 K.
Dynamic SRO breakdown nucleates HCP or amorphous regions at dislocation cores.
At temperatures above 900 K, thermal energy overcomes the activation barrier for rapid atomic diffusion.
Rapid atomic diffusion above 900 K causes SRO to collapse.
SRO normally pins dislocations in this alloy system.
Collapse of SRO causes a sudden decrease in stacking-fault energy.
The stacking-fault-energy decrease produces wide stacking faults that dissociate into partial dislocations.
The resulting partial dislocations annihilate or transform into HCP structures.
Loss of lattice periodicity facilitates amorphous shear-band formation.
Amorphous shear bands have high friction because they lack slip planes and exhibit increased adhesion.
From 300 K to 600 K, dislocation starvation or mechanical annealing decreases the friction coefficient.
Above 900 K, the friction spike will correlate with more than a 50% increase in HCP atom count and more than a 70% reduction in total dislocation line length.
Wear resistance drops precipitously when failure becomes dominated by shear bands.
Conventional thermal-softening models predict gradual decreases in hardness and friction with temperature because lattice friction decreases.
